Divide \([0,1]\) into \(n\) equal subintervals. Each one has width
\(\displaystyle \Delta x=\frac{b-a}{n}=\frac{1-0}{n}=\frac{1}{n}\)

The definite integral is the limit of the right-endpoint sums.
\(\displaystyle \int_{0}^{1}\left(-x^{2}\right)\,dx=\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=1}^{n}f(x_k)\,\Delta x\)

\(\displaystyle \Delta x=\frac{b-a}{n}=\frac{4-(-3)}{n}=\frac{7}{n}\)
The right endpoint of the \(k\)th subinterval is
\(\displaystyle x_k=a+k\,\Delta x=-3+k\cdot\frac{7}{n}=-3+\frac{7k}{n}\)
The definite integral is the limit of the right-endpoint sums.
\(\displaystyle \int_{-3}^{4}\left(2x^{2}-3x-7\right)\,dx=\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=1}^{n}f(x_k)\,\Delta x\)
Replace \(x_k\) and \(\Delta x\) with the expressions we just found.
\(\displaystyle \int_{-3}^{4}\left(2x^{2}-3x-7\right)\,dx=\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=1}^{n}\left[2\left(-3+\frac{7k}{n}\right)^{2}-3\left(-3+\frac{7k}{n}\right)-7\right]\frac{7}{n}\)
Multiply out the summand and write it as separate terms.
\(\displaystyle \int_{-3}^{4}\left(2x^{2}-3x-7\right)\,dx=\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=1}^{n}\left(\frac{140}{n}-\frac{735k}{n^{2}}+\frac{686k^{2}}{n^{3}}\right)\)
Pull each constant outside the sum. Then use these summation formulas.
\(\displaystyle \sum_{k=1}^{n}1=n\)
Adding 1 a total of n times gives n.
\(\displaystyle \sum_{k=1}^{n}k=\frac{n(n+1)}{2}\)
This is the sum of the first n counting numbers.
\(\displaystyle \sum_{k=1}^{n}k^{2}=\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}\)
This is the sum of the first n squares.
Substitute them into the sum.
\(\displaystyle \int_{-3}^{4}\left(2x^{2}-3x-7\right)\,dx=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left[\frac{140}{n}\cdot n-\frac{735}{n^{2}}\cdot \frac{n(n+1)}{2}+\frac{686}{n^{3}}\cdot \frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}\right]\)
Simplify the algebra so the expression involves only \(n\).
\(\displaystyle \int_{-3}^{4}\left(2x^{2}-3x-7\right)\,dx=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left[140-\frac{735}{2}\cdot \frac{n+1}{n}+\frac{343}{3}\cdot \frac{(n+1)(2n+1)}{n^{2}}\right]\)
To see what happens as \(n\) grows, split each fraction into separate terms.
\(\displaystyle \frac{n+1}{n}=1+\frac{1}{n}\)
\(\displaystyle \frac{(n+1)(2n+1)}{n^{2}}=2+\frac{3}{n}+\frac{1}{n^{2}}\)
\(\displaystyle \int_{-3}^{4}\left(2x^{2}-3x-7\right)\,dx=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left[140-\frac{735}{2}\cdot \left(1+\frac{1}{n}\right)+\frac{343}{3}\cdot \left(2+\frac{3}{n}+\frac{1}{n^{2}}\right)\right]\)
Now take the limit. As \(n\to\infty\), \(\frac{1}{n}\to 0\) and \(\frac{1}{n^{2}}\to 0\), so every term with \(n\) in the denominator vanishes.
\(\displaystyle \int_{-3}^{4}\left(2x^{2}-3x-7\right)\,dx=140-\frac{735}{2}\cdot \left(1+0\right)+\frac{343}{3}\cdot \left(2+0+0\right)\)
Simplify.
\(\displaystyle \int_{-3}^{4}\left(2x^{2}-3x-7\right)\,dx=\frac{7}{6}\)
